Bill (No. 162) to amend the Post Office Act-Mr, Lemieux-read a second time and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,
Hon. RODOLPHE LEMIEUX Postmaster General). This section of the Bill provides for a one cent postage rate in cities and towns where there is delivery by letter carriers. Formerly the one cent rate on what are commonly known as drop letters extended all over the Dominion, whe-

ther there was letter carrier delivery or not, but when a change in the law was made the rate was made two cents in cities and towns where there was delivery by letter carriers and it remained one cent at other post offices. This makes a universal rate of one cent for drop letters.
Mr. FOSTER Can the minister say to what extent the revenue will be affected by this ?

We have been influenced to make this change from the fact that iu large cities and towns the departmental stores, the manufacturing establishments and other concerns which do a large postal business, use the messenger service to dp-liver their letters as they found it cheaper, and in this way a large amount of revenue was lost to the post office.
Is that on account of the cheapness altogether or on account of the speed of delivery?

On account of the cheapness of the service. For instance, several firms will amalgamate their messenger service, employing, say, five or ten boys, to whom they will pay one cent or half a cent for each letter, and in that way they will make a profit. Of course, this action on their part is illegal, but it is one of these illegalities that we can hardly prosecute, and we thought it was better to adopt a uniform one cent rate, which we had formerly.
Do I understand the minister to say that it is illegal for a merchant to deliver his accounts by his own messenger?
Yes, in cities.
Provided only that they are sealed, not if they are delivered openly.

Certainly. My hon. [DOT]friend asked a question regarding the revenue. I will first lay down the principle that in all countries-Great Britain, Germany, France, the United States-whenever there has been a reasonable reduction in the rate of postage, there has been an immediate increase in the revenue. If the House will allow me I will give a few figures.
Of that postal revenue how much was derived from the two cent rate? .

In the report of last year it is stated that the stamp issue for the nine months ended the 31st March, 1907, represented a total of $5,094,347.75. a lit le more than half of our revenue. I should say that three-fourths of that amount is the product of the two-cent stamp, which is the one mostly used by the public. The stamps we have are half a cent, one cent, two cents, five cents, seven cents, ten cents, twenty cents and fifty cents.
Can the minister give ns any information as to the amount of money collected from the drop letters *delivered in the cities?

No. We have no statistics of that. We take the numter of letters that are received in the city post
offices, but we could not differentiate unless we took special statistics for one year.

How does the minister come to make the statement that the bulk of all this money is taken from the cities? I can quite understand that the letters are posted in the cities, but take the city of Winnipeg, which gives to the post office a revenue of over $500,000, a large share of that is for mail going to the rural districts.
Certainly.
Then the hon. gentleman was trying to show that the rural districts are giving no revenue to the Post Office Department.

The letters are posted to every section of the country, but it is in the cities where the revenue is collected. Let my hon. friend examine the offices in the last fiscal year. Take the offices' which give a revenue up to $1,000, the rural mail service is there carried on at the cost of a deficit of $143,723. Take the offices having a revenue of say $750 per year, they show a deficit in the mail service of $210,447.
Does the hon. minister think that is a fair comparison ?

It is out of the revenue obtained from the large cities that we pay for the maintenance of the rural service. How many offices do we not open in every section of the country just to accommodate small sections of the communities? Such offices give but little revenue, and the mail service costs a large amount because the distances are long. The revenue of the rural post offices do not compensate for the expenditure and maintenance of the rural mail service, but of course we have to maintain that service. To maintain it we get the money from the large cities. The cost of the mail service in the Yukon district is not far from $200,000 a year and the revenue is much below that figure.

I do not quite understand the minster's reasoning. He seems to take the position that if we had no rural districts, we would he better off financially speaking. But he would not get anything like the revenue he does from the large cities were it not for the rural districts. I would like to have an estimate of the amount paid for stamps and postage in the cities on mail matter that goes into the rural districts. If you take the statistics of the United States, you will find that 70 per cent of the mail in the rural districts originates in the cities. Take the city of Winnipeg, with its $500,000 or $600,000 income, if we were only distributing the mails in the city, there would not perhaps be half that amount brought into the Post Office Department. While the minister grants the

cities this drop letter system, whereby their letters can be delivered at one eent, he gives the rural districts no benefit. Why does he make the statement that the postal revenue would not be depreciated by the position he takes in connection with this measure? If the revenue is not going to depreciate to any extent, and he has had $1,500,000 of surplus the past year, what Will he do with the revenue?
Expand the service.

In what way? He will tell us that in some places he is establishing post offices every two miles, but does he think that will be of such wonderful benefit to the people of thickly settled districts? Would it hot be more reasonable to give those people rural free mail delivery?
I am not opposed to it but I say it will entail an immense expenditure.

The hon. minister is opposing it as much as he can, and the Minister of Agriculture has been telling the people what a staggering load free rural mail delivery would impose on them; and to bear out his argument he compares sparsely settled districts like the Yukon with the United States. I would like the minister to be fair in this matter and give the rural districts a square deal. If you are going to reduce the rates in the city to one cent, why not reduce the rate in the rural districts to one-half cent ? If you are going to have a million and a half that you do not know what to do with, and if you are not going to give a better service, why reduce the postage?

I am only giving to the cities where they have the letter carrier system what is already in existence in the rural districts. Every town, village and hamlet where they have not the letter-carrier system, have a one cent rate for drop letters. My hon. friend says we should do something for the rural districts. He knows that no reasonable request is refused, and, if he can trust me, he will find that no reasonable request will be refused in the future, for the rural section. The hon. gentleman speaks of the surplus. It is true, we have a surplus. I take some credit for keeping it. I am the trustee of the people-it is not my own money. I am not going to waste it uselessly, and be criticised by my hon. friend afterwards. I am going to spend it legitimately and honestly. Wherever a fair request is made for a better service in the country I will give it. I have already reduced the distances between post offices, and I intend to reduce them still further. I have increased the postmasters' salaries so that the minimum instead of being $25 is $35. I have increased the frequency of mail service-where a tri-weekly

service was found insufficient, I have made it a daily service, .and where a daily service was not enough, I have made it semi-daily. And I intend to go on in that way. My hon. friend speaks as though I were opposed to rural mail delivery. It is a splendid system, one that I admire greatly. If the Post Office Department in Canada had the means to give the people free rural mail delivery as they have it in the neighbouring Republic, I would give it with pleasure. But, with a territory as large as that of the United States, we have not the population, and we have a climate that is more severe. Besides we have not the revenue. But, step by step, the system will be established in Canada. There is a step towards rural mail delivery that is probably known to my hon. friend-it is the system known in the United States as the star route system. I do not say that I will not, after a careful examination, and after. consulting with my colleagues, try that system. But as I have told my hon. friend, we must not discriminate in the postal service. If we establish rural mail delivery, or the star route system in, say, the thickly-settled portions of his district in Ontario, how can I resist the demand that will be made by the members from the far west? The gentlemen who represent the far west in this House are just as much entitled to the system as those who represent the older districts of the east. However, that is not the question immediately before us. To answer my hon. friend as to the estimate of the revenue to follow this reduction, let me point out that the postage on domestic letters and letters to the United Slates was reduced from 3 cents to 2 cents on January 1, 1899 ; and, practically co-incident with that, at Christmas, 1898, the rate to Great Britain and the British colonies was reduced from 5 cents per half ounce to 2 cents. Tlie result of these reductions can be shown in a few figures. The revenue for the year 1898 was $3,527,810. In 1899, the revenue was $3,182,931, a reduction for the first year of the lower rate of postage of $344,879. But, in 1900, the revenue showed an increase of $1,053 above that of 1898. In 1901. tlie increase was $237,208, and in 1902. $466,934. Since then, it has increased by leaps and bounds. So, our experience is that a reduction in the rate of postage means an increase in the revenue. That is the experience of other countries also- there is no exception amongst progressive people. As I said a few weeks ago in answer to a question, there have been two great reductions in Canadian postage. In 1851, the rate was reduced from an average of 18 cents a letter to 6 cents per half ounce ; and, in 1868. it was reduced from 5 cents per half ounce to 3 cents per half ounce. In the former case, where the rates were reduced from 18 cents to 6 cents, the course of the revenue was as follows:-In

the first year, 1852, there was a decrease in the revenue of $131,436. But in 1853 there was an increase in the revenue of $47,000 in round figures; in 1854, $41,000; in 1855, $48,000. In 1868, after the reduction from 5 cents to 3 cents, the results were as follows In 1869, one year after, there was a decrease in the revenue of $51,646. But in 1870 and the following years there was a steady increase ; in the first year, $37,000, in the second year, $69,000. So although there was a reduction of 40 per cent, the revenue recovered itself in three years. I am quite positive, and that is the view taken by the oldest members of our staff, that even with the reduction, with the present prosperity in our large cities, we will get a material and substantial increase in our postal revenue, which increase will be used for the benefit of the rural sections of the country.
While the minister is making his explanations, perhaps he will tell us whether this financial superintendent is a new office.

Yes.
(Mr. URIAH WILSON. Would the hon. gentleman give us a full explanation of his duties, and tell us whether one man is expected to do all this?

I will first speak of the post office superintendent. According to our Post Office Act, a man who is appointed to the office of post office superintendent must have been in the service during a period of 10 years. We had decided to reduce that period to 5 years. We believe that a young man who has served five years is just as good and perhaps better fitted for that position than a man who has been 10 years in the service. But no man can be better fitted to fill the office of post office superintendent than the able gentleman is now filling that office, in the person of Mr. Ross, of Toronto, one of our oldest officers. I think it is a measure of prudence for the future to make this change. Now, as regards the question put by my hon. friend (Mr. Uriah Wilson) at present the financial inspection of the post offices, not only in the large cities but in the rural districts, is made part of the duties of our inspectors. As long as this inspection is confined to the rural sections of the country, our post office inspectors can do that work easily enough. But when it comes to the large offices in cities like Toronto, Montreal and Winnipeg, the case is different. The bookkeeping and generally speaking the collection of the revenue in those offices is much more complicated than it is in the rural sections of the country; therefore we find it desirable to appoint a man specially to have surveillance of those large offices, in order to protect both our revenue and our employees. We have several sources of revenue in those large offices; we have die
postal notes, the money orders, the amounts paid for transmission of papers and printed matter, and it taxes the ability of our inspectors, whose time is all taken up to the neglect sometimes of the rural districts.
Will one man do all this ?

We will have one man in Ottawa, and that man is at my left hand just now. He has been in the service for over 30 years. He was appointed by the Mackenzie government, and is one of the most expert accountants we have in the country. In view of the large revenue we are going to get, we think it necessary, in order to protect that revenue and to protect the employees in the city offices, to appoint a man to have direct surveillance over those matters.

I desire to say a few words with regard to this section. In the first place, I am in full accord with the minister's proposition to reduce the drop letter rate in cities. 'For my part I think that it never should have been raised. To my mind it is preposterous to charge two cents for the delivery of a letter across the street, and to charge only the same rate on a letter to Great Britain or to any of the colonies. It needs no argument to prove that. The basis of value should be service, and the delivery of a letter In the same city in which it is deposited should not be charged for at the same rate as when you send it across the continent or to a foreign country. It is only in recent years that this change was made. Take the city of Brantford where I live. Up to a few years ago our drop letters were one cent, and always had been. But seven or eight years ago the change was made, and the rate was advanced to two cents. At the same time the merchants continued to hold their boxes. We paid from $2 to $10 per annum rent for those boxes, and carried our own letters all the time. I myself, along with many other merchants, have always continued to carry our letters. We never see a postman on our premises from one years' end to the other. For reasons that are evident, we can get five or ten deliveries a day by carrying them ourselves. At the same time we continue to hold our boxes, and so we have been paying double rates. So in this respect the minister is only doing an act of justice. But in making the proposition he did tonight, I think he has misled the House, whether intentionally or not. But I wish to call the minister's attention to the laws and regulations of the postal department. I hold in my hand the Postal Guide, and I would direct his attention to page xxxv., clause 203. A few moments ago I asked him if he meant to say that it was an illegal act for a merchant to deliver his own accounts, and the minister promptly

replied that it was an illegal act. I did not think I misunderstood the minister. It was news to me but I did not like to contradict so eminent an authority without referring to the postal regulations. Clause 203 of the regulations reads:	.
The Postmaster General has the sole and exclusive privilege of conveying, receiving, collecting, sending and delivering letters within Canada; and (except in the oases hereinafter mentioned) any person who collects, sends, conveys, or delivers, or undertakes to convey or deliver, any letter within Canada, or who receives, or has in his possession any letter for the purpose of conveying or delivering It, otherwise than in conformity with the Post Office Act, for each and every letter so unlawfully conveyed or undertaken to be conveyed, received, delivered or found in his possession, is liable to a penalty not exceeding twenty dollars. The term letters as used in ths Act, is held to include circulars in the form of letters.
The following are the excepted cases:
ta) Letters sent by a private friend in his way, journey or travel, provided such letters be delivered by such friend to the party to whom they are addressed.
' (b) Letters sent by a messenger on purpose, concerning the private affairs of the sender or receiver.
(e) Commissions or returns thereof, and affidavits or writs, process or proceedings^ or returns thereof, issuing out of a court of justice.
(d) Letters addressed to a place out ot Canada, and sent bv sea and bv a private vessel.
.(e) Letters lawfully brought into Canada, and immediately posted at the nearest post office.
(f) Letters of merchants, owners of vessels of merchandise, or of the cargo or loading therein, sent by such vessel of merchandise, or hy any person employed by such owners for the carriage of such letters, according to their respective addresses, and delivered to the persons to whom they are respectively addressed, without pay, hire reward, advantage, or profit for so doing.
It is quite evident that the merchant is within his legal rights when he employs his own clerk or by bimself delivers his own bills or private letters or dunning letters. Tens of thousands are delivered in this way in the cities and it is perfectly legal.

I agree that the exceptions my hon. friend has just read only prove the excellence of the general rule. What I had in mind was the clubbing of merchants, manufacturers and insurance men In the cities to have a messenger service for the delivery of their letters and accounts. That is clearly illegal.

I was going to support the minister, but be took the ground away from me by his statement that the practice of delivering letters in this way, which I myself have followed, was illegal. I think he is right in this proposal and that he is justified in the hope that a large amount of mail matter now delivered in Mr. COCKSHUTT.
this way will be posted. The bulk of the postage after all originates in the cities, although, of course, much of it goes to the country. The average citizen of the town or city writes five or ten letters to the one written by the man in the country. The postage on the monthly accounts and the circulars sent out by merchants comes to a tremendous amount and no doubt much more of tbis class of matter will be sent under tbis reduction. We can deliver these letters at half a cent, and merchants will still probably deliver a considerable portion of this class of correspondence because a boy can earn $2 to $3 a day delivering letters or accounts at half a cent apiece The Postmaster General is doing an act of justice in this and I trust his estimate of returns will be fulfilled.

I am quite In sympathy with tbis proposed reduction. I cannot agree with the Postmaster General's statement that the city revenue pays for the country service. Without the country the city revenue would not amount to much.
I do not deny that.
Consequently his statement Is not fair to the country.

The hon. member is quite right in saying that no distinction should be made between the rural sections and the cities; what I have in mind is that the revenue originates in the cities. Certainly a large amount of postage stamps are bought to send letters into the country districts. Take Eaton in Toronto, one of our best clients, who buys probably $100,000 worth of stamps, all his postage is for the country districts.

The city revenue would certainly not be so large were it not for the country custom which the city people have. Looking at it in that light, whilst I justify the Postmaster General in the reduction he proposes on city letters, I contend that in all other districts where there is no such delivery there should be a corresponding reduction and it is my intention, when the Postmaster General has adopted his clause reducing the postage on the drop letters in cities, to move an amendment which will have the effect of reducing the postage in the rural districts and in all places where there is no delivery by mail carrier, from one cent to one-half cent.
Going us one better.

I think the proportion is fair, that the country is entitled to that if the city is to get the other. The Postmaster General may think I come from the country. Possibly I do and I am not ashamed of it. I have respect for the people who live on the land and I want to stand for their rights. I think the Post-

master General should have conceded this point at the same time as he conceded the other. This is not the first time I have called his attention to this matter.

I would ask my hon. friend (Mr. Henderson) to be good enough to withdraw his amendment and to leave the rural section of the country to my tender mercy. Let us first try the one cent drop letter, and if as a result the revenue increases, as I feel quite certain it will, then I shall give my hon. friend's amendment yer- serious consideration. Will the hon. gentleman trust me for one year or perhaps two?
I would gladly take the suggestion of the Postmaster General if I were sure he would be Postmaster General next year.
If I am not, my hon. friend (Mr. Henderson) may be, and then he will carry out his own policy.

I made up my mind some time ago that when the opportunity arose I would move this amendment. I would like to know what the House and the country thinks of it, and the Postmaster General will also learn the feeling of the people on the question, a fact which may be of advantage to him. I would gladly accept the suggestion of the Postmaster General, but I made a promise to myself to move this amendment and although I have every respect for the hon. gentleman still I must respect myself. My amendment is :
Moved by Mr. Henderson seconded by Mr. Elain-
That section 48 of the Post Office Act is amended by inserting the word 'half' after the word ' one * in the third line of said section, and by inserting in the fifth line the words ' in cases where there is no delivery by letter carrier.'
The net result of the amendment is that outside of the plnces where there is a letter carrier delivery there shall be a half cent rate instead of a one cent rate as at present.

Will my hon. triend leave this as a notice of motion until next year? I fear it is I who am the Conservative to-night and that my hon. friend is the Radical, for we must not all at once revolutionize the whole postal system. Let us wait for a year or two to see what the result of the present reduction will be and if the increase of the past few years continues it is my intention to give further postal reductions. Of course as to that I would have to consult my colleagues.

I entirely disagree with the view expressed by the Postmaster Genera] to-night that the larger proportion of the postal revenue originates in the towns and cities. In my opinion nearly all of the revenue which the towns contribute comes from the country. The correspondence from the city is addressed to the people of the country and the parcels are sent to people living in the country, and in the long run it is they who are the producers of the wealth who pay the postage. I would be much more disposed to depend on the assurance of the Postmaster General if I thought he had a proper idea as to the proportionate contributions between the towns and the country districts to the postal revenue. I believe the proposal of the hon. gentleman from Halton is a proper one and I trust the minister will seriously take it into consideration.

In this proposal the Postmaster General is most certainly discriminating against the rural districts. When he says that Mr. Eaton, of Toronto, is returning to the postal department a revenue of $100,000 per annum he must remember that a large proportion of that comes from the people of the rural districts to whom he sends his goods and his circulars. As to a rural mail delivery the minister does not seem to realize that the thickly settled portions of the rural districts of Canada are not any different from the thickly settled portions of the United States and that in the United States there are sparsely settled districts as there are in Canada. The minister knows they do not have rural free delivery in the sparsely settled districts of the United States, and why he basis his argument on the 6,000,000 people in Canada and the 80,000,000 in the United States I cannot understand.

I want to make a suggestion to the Postmaster General as to better rural mail delivery than we have. He is making a change in the postal arrangements for the benefit of the cities; but, while I am in favour of every reduction in the postal rates, whether it be in the city or the country, still I think the Postmaster General might direct his attention to improving the rural mail service. In my own county there are some sections which only get a mail twice a week; so I am informed in letters from my constituency. 1 think one of the aims of the Postmaster General should he to rectify grievances of that kind. I think every section of Ontario should have a daily mail wherever it is possible.

This is the first time I have heard any complaint in regard to the mail service in my hon. friend's riding. Whenever he can point out any deficiency in the service. I shall be only too pleased to rectify it.

I appreciate that very much and I will make inquiry and if I find that the grievance which I have mentioned is a reality, I will call the Postmaster General's

attention to it in the hope that he will rectify it.	,

After having heard the very strong assurance which the Postmaster General has given us, I think that my purpose will possibly be more likely to be accomplished by not pressing my amendment than by pressing it. X have no desire to embarrass the Postmaster General in this matter. I might perhaps gain a little political capital by pressing it; but my desire is to get the reduction in postage, which is of more importance than any petty party advantage I might gain. Therefore after the Postmaster General's statement, I am quite willing to allow the matter to stand over.

I can assure my hon. friend that my promise to take the matter into very serious consideration is not a vain promise, and my hon. friend may remind me of it at any time. I am only too pleased in postal matters to give the best possible facilities to the people; and if any further reduction can be given, which is reasonable and acceptable to the government and the House, I shall certainly bow before public opinion.

A few days ago there was a little discussion regarding the mail service on the Murray harbour branch of the Prince Edward Island Railway, and the minister promised to confer with the Minister of Railways and Canals in reference to it. I think this would be a fitting opportunity to put the question again.

Yes, and I am pleased to embalm the answer in the columns of [DOT] Hansard.' The other day my hon. friend called my attention to the wretched mail service on the Prince Edward Island Railway, and the day afterwards I made clippings of the matter from ' Hansard ' and wrote a letter to the Minister of Railways and Canals. I have received an answer from him, and if my hon. friend will put a question on the Order Paper or move for that correspondence, I shall be pleased to bring it down. The Minister of Railways and Canals has promised me that he will take up the question as soon as he visits Prince Edward Island, as he intends to do this summer. There is not only the question of the mail service; there is the question of the whole rearrangement of the railway service. As regards the mail service, we are prepared to give the best service possible provided we are helped by the Railway Department.
Will the minister lay the correspondence on the table of the House, as I cannot move for it at the present time?
I will let my hon. friend have a copy.
I understood the Postmaster General to say that the distance between rural post offices had been reduced. What is the distance now?

I will not say that there is a fixed distance; but the average distance was between seven and eight miles. When I have an application at a distance of three miles or even two miles, where there is a dense population, I grant the request by giving the post office apd extending the service.
On section 2,
Will the Postmaster General state exactly what this second clause is to cover ?

The post office superintendent, Mr. Ross of Toronto, has filled that office quite ably for thirty-five years. He has the general supervision of all the post offices of the Dominion. He travels from one end of the country to the other. His powers are second only to those of the Deputy Postmaster General. In fact, he acts for the Deputy Postmaster General all over the Dominion. I may say that Mr. Ross is filling the position quite ably, and hope he will continue to fill it for a long time. But at present we have to take an officer who has served at least ten years in the Post Office Department to fill that position.
I wish to reduce that to five years, so that for the future we can avail ourselves of the services of younger men, when we select a successor to Mr. Ross.

I do not think that is in the interest of the service. It takes away from civil servants who have learned their business, and worked their way up to be good and efficient servants, the opportunity to fill one of the highest offices in the service. I think it is a great pity to make such a change as this.

We are only reducing the number of years in the service. A man must still be taken direct from the department. When a man has been in the department from the age of thirty years to the age of forty years, he may have lost his grip. I am in favour of young men in the service as much as possible. If after five years service a young man is not able to show his ability, he will not be able to show it any better after ten years.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.
